Surah al-Shams is Meccan, and it has fifteen verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

By the sun and its brightness, / By the moon when it follows it, / By the day when it displays it, / By the night when it covers it, / By the heaven and He who built it, / By the earth and He who spread it out, / By the soul and He who proportioned it, / And inspired it with its wickedness and its piety, / He has indeed succeeded who purifies it, / And he has indeed failed who corrupts it. / Thamud denied in their transgression, / When the most wretched of them was sent forth, / Then the Messenger of Allah said to them: "The she-camel of Allah, and her drink." / But they denied him and hamstrung her, so their Lord crushed them for their sin and leveled them, / And He does not fear its consequence.

Ṭaḥā and daḥā have one meaning: he spread out and smoothed. Ṭaḥā may also mean "went away," as in the words of ʿAlqama:

*Ṭaḥā bika qalbun fī al-ḥisān ṭarūb*

It is also said: "I do not know where it ṭaḥā," meaning where it went; this was said by Abu ʿAmr. In the oaths of the Arabs: "No, by the moon al-ṭāḥī," meaning the one that rises high in the east. It is also said: ṭaḥā yaṭḥū ṭaḥwan, and yaṭḥā ṭaḥwan.

Al-tadsiyah means concealment. Its root is dassa, and the third of the doubled letters was replaced by a weak letter, as they said in naqṣuṣ / naquṣṣ. The poet said:

*Wa-anta alladhī dassasta ʿAmran fa-aṣbaḥat ḥalāʾiluhu minhu arāmila ṣuyʿā*

It is also recited:

*Wa-dassasta ʿAmran fī al-turāb*

Dammama ʿalayhi al-qabr: he closed it over him. Muʾarrij said: al-dammama is destruction by uprooting. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it says: "I dammamtu the thing": I stuck it to the ground and flattened it.

This surah is Meccan. Since the oaths earlier concerned certain noble places and what follows them, here He swears by something of the upper world and the lower world, and by that which is the instrument of reflection on these, namely the soul. The preceding surah closed with something of the condition of the disbelievers in the Hereafter, so this one closes with something of their condition in this world, which corresponds to their fate in the Hereafter, the Fire, and in this world, to total destruction. The discussion of ḍuḥā has already been covered in Surat Ṭāhā at His words: "And that the people be gathered in the forenoon" (20:59). Mujahid said: it is the rising and perfection of light. Muqatil said: its heat, based on His words: "nor are you exposed to the sun's heat" (20:119). Qatada said: it is the whole day, but this is not good, because He has sworn by the day. The known meaning in the language is that ḍuḥā is shortly after the sunrise; when it extends, it is ḍaḥāʾ, with a long vowel and a fatḥa on the ḍād, until midday. Muqatil's statement is an explanation by a necessary consequence. As for what is reported from al-Mubarrad, that ḍuḥā is derived from al-ḍiḥḥ, which is the light of the sun, with the alif transposed from the second ḥāʾ, and likewise the waw in ḍaḥwa is transposed from the second ḥāʾ, perhaps this is fabricated against him, because al-Mubarrad is too exalted to hold this; these are two different roots, and one cannot be derived from the other.

"By the moon when it follows it." Al-Ḥasan and al-Farrāʾ said: talāhā means it follows it constantly at every time, because it receives its light from it, so it follows it for this reason. Ibn Zayd said: it follows it throughout the month: in the first half of the month by rising, and in the latter by setting. Ibn Sallam said: in the first half of the month, because it takes its place and travels behind it; when the sun sets, the moon rises following it. Qatada said: that refers only to the full moon, when the sun sets and the moon rises. Al-Zajjāj and others said: talāhā means it became full and round, and it followed the sun in light and measure, because among the stars there is nothing that follows the sun in this sense except the moon. It was also said: from the beginning of the month to its middle, at sunset the sun sets and then the moon sets; in the latter half they alternate, so that the sun sets and the moon rises. Al-Zamakhshari said: talāhā means rising as it sets, taking from its light, and that is in the first half of the month.

"By the day when it displays it." The apparent meaning is that the object of jallāhā is the pronoun referring to the sun, because when the day spreads out, the sun becomes fully manifest at that time. It was also said: it refers to the darkness; or to the earth; or to the world. What clears the darkness is the sun or the day, for even if the sun does not rise, the darkness does not remain. The subject of jallāhā is the pronoun of the day. It was said that it may refer to Allah, as if He said: "By the day when Allah displays the sun," so He swears by the day in its most perfect states.

"By the night when it covers it." That is, it covers the sun, so by its entry the sun sets and the horizons grow dark; ascribing this to the night is metaphorical. It was said the pronoun refers to the earth. What eloquence requires is that all the pronouns up to His words "it covers it" refer to the sun. Just as the day displayed it, so the day is what covers it. Since the verse endings were arranged upon the alif and the feminine hā', He used the present tense in "by the night when it covers it," because that is the state in which the arrangement is set; had He used the past tense, as in what precedes and follows, the phrasing would be "when it covered it," and the verse ending would be lost, though it is intended. Al-Qaffal said, in summary: these oaths by the sun are in reality according to four attributes: its light at the height of the day, at the time animals spread out and seek livelihood; the moon following it by taking its light; the completion of its rising and emergence; and its setting with the coming of night.

As for "what" in "and what built it," "and what spread it," "and what proportioned it," it is in the sense of "He who," as said by al-Ḥasan, Mujahid and Abu ʿUbayda, and chosen by al-Ṭabarī; they said that "mā" can refer to those of knowledge and to others. It was also said to be a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), said by Qatada, al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjāj; this is the view of those who hold that "mā" does not refer to individual rational beings.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it was made maṣdariyya, but this is not the right view because of His words "so He inspired it," and what would follow from it of corruption of the composition. The right view is that it is relative (mawṣūla), and it was preferred over "man" to convey the sense of description, as if it were said: "and the heaven and the Mighty Powerful who built it, and the soul and the Wise, Overwhelming in wisdom, who proportioned it." And in their speech: "Glory be to Him who subjected this to us." End.

As for his saying that it is not the right view because of "so He inspired it," meaning that the pronoun in "so He inspired it" returns to Allah, so it would return to something mentioned, namely what is meant by "alladhī," this does not necessarily follow; for when we make it maṣdariyya, the pronoun returns to what is understood from the context of speech. Thus in "built it" there is a pronoun referring to Allah, i.e., "and He built it," as when you see Zayd has struck ʿAmr and say: "I marvelled at what struck ʿAmr," its estimate being: "who struck ʿAmr?" This is good, eloquent and permissible, and the return of a pronoun to what is understood from the context is common. His saying that it leads to corruption of composition is not so, and making it maṣdariyya does not lead to what he mentioned. His saying "it was preferred... etc." does not mean by "mā" or "man" the descriptive sense, because these two relative pronouns are not described by it, unlike "alladhī"; so their shared lack of the descriptive sense is present in both, and "mā" does not uniquely have it apart from "man." As for his saying "in their speech... etc.," our companions interpreted it as meaning that "subḥāna" is a proper name and "mā" is a temporal maṣdariyya.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, the matter of the accusative of *idhā* is difficult, for either you make the *wāws* conjunctive and govern with them the accusative and genitive, falling into conjunction over two governors, as in your saying: "I passed yesterday by Zayd and today by ʿAmr," or you make them oaths, and fall into what al-Khalīl and Sibawayh agreed is disliked. I say: the answer is that the *wāw* of oath is used with the verb being wholly omitted, so it has a status different from the *bāʾ*, with which the verb is expressed or implied; the *wāw* stands in place of the verb, and the *bāʾ* serves in place of both together. The conjunctive *wāws* are substitutes for this, so they should govern both the verb and the preposition, as you say: "Zayd struck ʿAmr and Bakr struck Khālid," where you raise with the *wāw* and put in the accusative, because it stands in place of "struck" which governs both. End.

As for his saying about conjunctive *wāws*, that it governs in the accusative and genitive by them, this is not the preferred view; that is, that the conjunctive particle governs by standing in place of the governor, rather the preferred view is that the governing belongs to the governor of the conjoined noun, and the evidence of the practice supports this. As for his saying that it falls into conjunction over two governors, what is in the verse is not conjunction over two governors, but rather conjunction of a noun in the genitive and a noun in the accusative over a noun in the genitive and a noun in the accusative, so the conjunctive particle does not take the place of two governors. This is like your saying: "Pass by Zayd standing and ʿAmr sitting." Sibawayh has quoted in his book:

*Fa-laysa bi-maʿrūfin lanā an nuraddahā ṣiḥāḥan wa-lā mustankarin an tuʿaqqarā*

Here is conjunction of a genitive and nominative over a genitive and nominative, and conjunction over two governors has four views, and permission has been attributed to Sibawayh. His saying, "like your saying: I passed yesterday by Zayd and today by ʿAmr," this example differs from what is in the verse; rather the pattern of the verse is: "I passed by Zayd yesterday and by ʿAmr today," and we permit this. As for his saying "falls into what is disliked," this is not as he stated; rather the words of al-Khalīl indicate prohibition.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that they be a group, and the singular is for your equating in the superlative when you add it between the singular and plural, and the masculine and feminine, and it would have been permissible to say: "أشقوْها" (ashqawhā). End of quotation. He applied the addition without restriction, and he should have said "to a definite noun," because its addition to an indefinite noun is not permissible at that time, except that it be singular masculine, as is its condition when it is with مَن. The apparent reference of the pronoun in (لهم) [al-Shams: 13] is to the nearest preceding mention, which is (أشقاها) if a group is intended, and it may refer to (ثمود). (رسول) is Salih (peace be upon him).

The majority recited ﴿the she-camel of Allah﴾ [al-Shams: 13] with a fatḥa on the tāʾ, and it is accusative as a warning against what the operator must be supposed to govern, because it has been conjoined to it, so its ruling by conjunction becomes the ruling of the repeated element, as in your saying: "The lion, the lion!" meaning: "Beware of the she-camel of Allah and her drink, so do not do that." (فكذّبوه) [al-Shams: 14]: the majority hold that they were disbelievers. It is also reported that they had embraced Islam before that and followed Salih for a period, then they denied him and hamstrung the camel. The hamstringing is attributed to the group because they were content with it and in collusion over it.

The majority recited (فَدَمْدَمَ) [al-Shams: 14] with a mīm after two dāls, while Ibn al-Zubayr recited (فدهدم) with a hāʾ between them, meaning He closed the punishment over them, repeating it upon them. (بذنبهم) [al-Shams: 14] contains a warning of the consequence of sins. (فَسَوّاها) [al-Shams: 14]: it was said: He leveled the tribe in destruction, returning to it with the feminine, just as it returned in (بطغواها). It was also said: He leveled the destruction, meaning He made it equal among them, so that none of them escaped, small or great. Ubayy, al-Aʿraj, Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmir recited (فلا يخاف) [al-Shams: 15] with a fāʾ, and the rest of the seven recited (ولا) with a wāw. The pronoun in (يخاف) most apparently refers to the nearest preceding mention, which is their Lord, meaning there is no pursuer (دَرَك) over Him, Exalted, in His action toward them; He is not questioned about what He does. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan, and in it is a rebuke of them and a pursuit of their traces. It was also said: It may refer to Salih, meaning he did not fear the consequence of this deed toward them, since he had warned and cautioned them. Whoever recited (ولا) cannot have the pronoun allow both interpretations. Al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Muqatil, al-Zajjaj and Abu ʿAli said: the wāw is the wāw of the circumstantial state (واو الحال), and the pronoun in (يخاف) refers to (أشقاها), meaning: he went out to hamstring her, while he did not fear the consequence of his deed because of his disbelief and transgression. The consequence (العقبى) is the end of a thing and what comes after it as a result. This has remoteness because of the long separation between the circumstantial state and its owner.
